segment_name: Opening: Money, Dust, and the Thames

questions.question: Oliver, you've said that once you hear these scenes performed, something clicks that you can't get off the page alone. Can you take us into that grindstone moment — the mime outside the keyhole — and show us what you mean? What does Dickens actually do with the sound and the silence there?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform or close-read the grindstone passage, setting up the 'pecuniary swoon' and the silent laugh as anchors for the whole segment — and give Edmund and Daniel something concrete to respond to

questions.question: Daniel, you said something in our chat that's stuck with me — that Dickens 'refuses to let you feel sorry for anyone' in this opening. But Oliver just made it sound almost warm, almost fond. Is Dickens delighting in these men or exposing them? Can he be doing both at once?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Daniel's structural coldness reading and Oliver's humane-grotesque reading — get them to fight over whether Dickens's comedy is compassionate or diagnostic

questions.question: Edmund, you're going to fight both of them on this, I suspect. Because you're saying the system isn't the point — the choices are. Wegg has a wooden leg, he's been dealt a bad hand, Daniel wants to ask what made him this way. What's your answer to that question?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's strongest take on individual will versus structural determinism, and provoke a direct exchange with Daniel on whether Wegg is villain or symptom

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund just said the wooden leg is 'the physical token of how Wegg's choices have maimed him.' That's a very particular reading. You've called the same leg a dehumanizing instrument of capitalist appetite. Who's right about the leg?
questions.intent: Make the wooden leg the concrete focal point of the Edmund vs Daniel disagreement — forces both to commit to a close reading rather than staying abstract, should produce genuine argument

questions.question: Last one — and I want to pull us to that other passage, the father with the faltering hands. Oliver, you said there's something deliberately enigmatic about him, that 'curious glance,' that he might know more than he's letting on. Edmund thinks he's a portrait of shame and dissolution. Daniel thinks he's a creature of the system. Is there a version of this scene where all three of you are looking at the same man?
questions.intent: Bring the three readings into collision on a single image — the father's trembling hands — and push toward a synthesis or a cleaner statement of irreconcilable difference to close the segment on

steering_notes: The three readings are genuinely in tension and that's the engine here: Oliver wants warmth and performance, Edmund wants moral seriousness and individual agency, Daniel wants structural critique and refuses sentiment. Don't let them settle into agreement too quickly — the wooden leg is the best concrete object to keep returning to when the conversation gets too abstract. Push for close reading over theory wherever possible. If Daniel gets too systemic, bring him back to the text. If Edmund gets too moralistic, ask him to point to the line. Oliver is the natural mediator but also the one most likely to say something surprising — give him room.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that 'the dust is just dust' directly contradicts Daniel's reading of the dust heap as a symbol of capitalist circulation — worth surfacing if the conversation opens up beyond the Wegg passages

Oliver and Daniel both want to quote 'pecuniary swoon' but for almost opposite reasons: Oliver finds delight and humane comedy, Daniel finds honest exposure of money-hunger stripped of moral language — make them say why their readings diverge on the same three words

Edmund's insistence that Wegg's wooden leg is a 'token of his choices' is a direct provocation to Daniel's structural reading and to Oliver's bodily-grotesque reading — the leg is the best cross-engagement object in the segment

Oliver's point about the father's 'curious glance' being enigmatic cuts against both Edmund's shame-reading and Daniel's institution-of-shame reading — if Oliver develops this, the other two should be asked to respond directly

segment_name: The Art of Deception: Harmon's Masquerade and Narrative Sleight of Hand

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our chat that I can't stop thinking about — that Dickens isn't trying to fool us, he's trying to control *exactly what kind of attention* we're paying. Can you read us the oakum whiskers passage from chapter 30 and tell us what you hear when you read it? Because to me it sounds less like a novelist and more like a stage manager calling cue.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read c30:p3 aloud and open the theatrical performance argument, setting up the central question of whether this is craft or confession

questions.question: Daniel, I want to push you on something. Trevelyan's just said the pleasure is in the *performance* of transformation — the oakum hair comes off, and there's a kind of delight in watching it happen. But you're saying that same moment is actually the novel showing us something disturbing: that Harmon can only survive by becoming someone else entirely. How do you square that? Is Dickens celebrating a trick or accidentally confessing a crime?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to directly engage with Trevelyan's theatrical reading using c30:p3, and draw out the class-mobility argument about identity erasure as structural rather than romantic

questions.question: Edmund, I know you're itching to get into the Boffins here, because both Daniel and Oliver have used that scene — Mrs Boffin's bonnet spinning across the yard after young John knocks it off — for completely different purposes. Daniel sees it as evidence of precarity and patronage, Oliver sees it as grotesque comedy that earns the later masquerade. You want to read it to us and tell us what *you* think Dickens is actually doing in that room?
questions.intent: Get Leigh to read c8:p39 aloud and make the moral-imagination argument; the direct contrast with Rosen's structural reading should produce genuine disagreement

questions.question: All three of you have mentioned the moment where Dickens basically breaks cover in the postscript — 'I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers would suppose I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest.' Edmund, you read that as Dickens the moralist scolding us for caring more about being fooled than about being transformed. But Daniel thinks it's Dickens *apologizing* for doing what the class system does — hiding violence under sentiment. Oliver thinks it's a showman taking a bow. Can all three of you be right? Or does one of those readings actually kill the others?
questions.intent: Create a three-way collision on c67:p57 — the passage everyone wants to use — and force the experts to adjudicate between moral, structural, and theatrical interpretations

questions.question: Daniel, I want to give you the last word on this before we move on, because you said something that I think is the most provocative claim of the whole conversation: that the masquerade proves there *is* no true identity under capitalism, only the performance of position — and that Dickens can't quite let himself think it through, so he resolves it sentimentally. Edmund is going to disagree with you violently. So make your case: is Harmon's return to himself a redemption, or is it just a costume change with better tailoring?
questions.intent: Draw out Rosen's strongest and most confrontational take — the 'unconscious critique' argument — and explicitly invite Leigh to respond, creating the segment's climactic disagreement

steering_notes: This segment has a genuine three-way split that's worth exploiting rather than smoothing over: Leigh wants moral redemption, Trevelyan wants theatrical pleasure, Rosen wants structural critique. The sweet spot is making each of them feel the others are *missing something real* rather than simply wrong — that produces better radio than a debate. Push the reading-aloud moments hard: all three passages (c30:p3, c8:p39, c67:p57) are short enough to quote on air and specific enough to anchor abstract arguments. Watch for Leigh and Rosen to talk past each other on the Boffin scene — they're describing the same passage but seeing completely different things, and that's worth slowing down. Don't let Trevelyan retreat into 'it's all of those things' synthesis — he has a real argument about performance and form that's distinct from both the others, and he should be pushed to defend it against Rosen's structural reading specifically.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that Harmon's perfect disguise proves identity is 'entirely malleable' directly contradicts Leigh's claim that Harmon *is* Rokesmith because he *chooses* to be good — this is the segment's sharpest disagreement and should be named explicitly on air

Trevelyan reads Charley's confrontation with Bradley (c57:p80) as fragile and frightened; Rosen reads the same passage as evidence that social position depends entirely on vouching by those already inside the system — both are plausible and incompatible, worth a quick detour if time allows

All three experts want to use c67:p57 but for opposite purposes: Leigh as moral rebuke, Trevelyan as showman's bow, Rosen as authorial confession of complicity — having them each read a clause of it in sequence could be a strong radio moment

Rosen's structural reading of Riah's kindness (c22:p139) as 'evidence of bankruptcy' is the direct inverse of Trevelyan's reading of it as 'the one true thing in a novel of false faces' — this complementary opposition is worth surfacing if the segment has momentum

segment_name: Golden Dustman: Boffin's Conscience and the Corruption of Wealth

questions.question: Edmund, let's start with the passage that everyone seems to want to quote — the Secretary's line about the begging letters, 'what minced veal is to a calf.' You read that as brilliant Augustan wit, anatomy of human folly. But here's what I want to push on: the Secretary is employed by the Boffins to *filter* these people. He's not a satirist — he's a functionary. Does the comedy let us off the hook a bit too easily?
questions.intent: Get Leigh to commit hard to the literary-moralist reading before Rosen can land the structural critique. Forces him to defend the comedy as morally neutral.

questions.question: Daniel, you've basically said the opposite — that the minced veal line is where Dickens is *most* precise about how the whole social order has become a machine of parasitism. But Edmund would say you're turning Dickens into a sociologist he didn't want to be. So I want you to make the case: what's actually in those passages — c17:p4 and c17:p5 — that tells you this is systemic critique and not just very funny characterisation?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to do close reading rather than theoretical assertion — get him to the 'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet' line and explain why the *form* of that prose is ideological, not just comic.

questions.question: Oliver, you've got a third position here that I find genuinely strange and I want to test it. You're saying the real corruption isn't moral and it isn't systemic — it's about *visibility*. The moment you have money, you become a text everyone wants to rewrite. But doesn't that risk making the Boffins' suffering a bit too aesthetic? The begging letters are funny. The minced veal line is funny. Are you saying the comedy itself is the corruption?
questions.intent: Draw out Trevelyan's most original take — the visibility thesis — and push him to articulate how the performative satire and the moral tragedy are actually the same thing. Should produce genuine surprise from the other two.

questions.question: Edmund, here's the passage I want to bring in now — c9:p29, where the narrator tells us the Boffins have a 'genuine religious duty' and celebrates them almost tenderly. Oliver's pre-show argument is that Dickens the entertainer quietly undermines what Dickens the moralist claims here. Do you think the novel *earns* that narrator's confidence in the Boffins, or is there a gap between what we're told and what we see?
questions.intent: Set up the Trevelyan-Leigh fault line: does the novel endorse its own moral thesis? Gets Leigh to defend the narrator's sincerity, which Trevelyan will then complicate.

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you in on this — Daniel, you called Harmon's 'shrinking from my father's money' in c30:p7 a fantasy of moral innocence, a performance. Edmund thinks it's a portrait of genuine personal scruple. Oliver thinks it's a man trying on identities who's already compartmentalised. So who's right about what that repetition — 'shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory' — is actually *doing*? Is Dickens endorsing Harmon's discomfort, or is he watching it with some irony?
questions.intent: Bring all three into direct confrontation over the same passage. The question of whether Harmon's anxiety is sincere, ironic, or structurally impotent is the sharpest three-way split in the room — this should generate genuine argument.

steering_notes: The productive fault line in this segment runs between Leigh's moralism, Rosen's structuralism, and Trevelyan's strange third category — the corruption of visibility and performance. Don't let Rosen and Leigh fight each other to a draw on the social-versus-individual question without pulling Trevelyan's take in, because it cuts across both of them. The minced veal line is the shared text — all three want it — so use it early as a Rorschach test to establish how differently they're reading even when they agree on the quote. The c30:p7 Harmon passage is the best three-way collision point and should come last, when the room is warm. Keep Leigh from retreating into Burke — if he invokes tradition or organicism, redirect to the specific text.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that the Secretary's disgust in c17:p4-5 'masks complicity' directly contradicts Leigh's reading of the same passage as literary wit with no political edge — get them talking to each other about the *same words* rather than different frameworks

Trevelyan's visibility thesis (wealth corrupts through being seen) is actually a synthesis of Leigh and Rosen that neither has fully considered — Leigh might be surprised to find it compatible with moral testing, Rosen might find it too aesthetic

All three cite the 'Evil often stops short' passage from different angles: Leigh reads it straight as moral thesis, Rosen reads it as ironic, Trevelyan doesn't mention it — this is a point to open up mid-segment if energy drops

Rosen and Trevelyan agree that Harmon's 'shrinking' is in some sense performative but for completely different reasons — Rosen sees structural impotence, Trevelyan sees identity performance. Leigh disagrees entirely. This three-way split on a single word is excellent radio.

segment_name: Bella's Reckoning: From Mercenary to Human

questions.question: Oliver, you've described Bella as essentially an actress — she changes costume, she changes register, the prose around her physically shifts. But here's what I want to push on: is there actually a *self* underneath all the performance? Or is Dickens just swapping one performance for another when she accepts poverty?
questions.intent: Open the central tension between performance and transformation; get Oliver to articulate the 'mechanical men' thesis and Bella as the one who breaks the machine; sets up Edmund's counter about genuine conversion of the will

questions.question: Edmund, I want to go to that moment in c49:p74 — R. Wilfer and the 'mercenary young person distantly related to myself.' You said this is the novel's real centre, not the romance. Can you read us that passage and tell me why a stammering father repeating himself is doing more moral work than anything else in the book?
questions.intent: Get the passage read aloud for radio; draw out Edmund's take that this is individual moral conversion rather than social comment; sets up the direct collision with Daniel who thinks Wilfer is blessing economic submission dressed as wisdom

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund is going to say that's a father watching his daughter choose love over money — a genuine moral victory. You're going to say that's a father blessing his daughter for accepting powerlessness. But here's the thing that bothers me about your reading: Dickens gives us that extraordinary line in c18:p149 — 'if she ever had one, Charley' — which really *does* treat poverty as structural horror. So why does he then turn around and make Bella's acceptance of smallness into triumph? Is he confused, or is he doing something more calculated than that?
questions.intent: Force Daniel to commit to whether the ideological contradiction is Dickens's blindspot or his sleight of hand; create the sharpest possible clash with Edmund's moral reading and Oliver's theatrical one

questions.question: Let's go to c30:p22 — Harmon deciding to 'prove Bella' while hiding in a public house. Oliver, you said the text *knows* this is manipulative, that Dickens is testing us, not vindicating John. Daniel thinks it's a straightforward patriarchal fantasy. Edmund thinks it's the novel's deepest question about whether character can be tested at all. Who's right? Because the passage can't sustain all three readings simultaneously — can it?
questions.intent: Force a three-way collision on the novel's most morally ambiguous plot mechanism; get the experts responding to each other rather than just making separate points; keep energy combative and fast

questions.question: Final question, Edmund, and I want everyone to weigh in: you said Bella's reckoning is with herself, not with society. Daniel says she's internalizing poverty as virtue. Oliver says she's refusing the script. Are any of those three things actually different? Or is Dickens doing all three at once — and if he is, does that make the novel richer or does it make it a muddle?
questions.intent: Force synthesis or irresolvable disagreement as a closing move; good radio ending because it either produces a surprising consensus or a productive three-way standoff; lets the strongest takes clash on equal terms

steering_notes: Keep Daniel's structural critique and Edmund's moral reading in collision throughout — they are the sharpest poles. Oliver is the most useful moderating voice but has his own strong thesis (theatrical reversal, mechanical men) that shouldn't get lost between the other two. Make sure c18:p149 gets read aloud — that 'if she ever had one' conditional is the best single phrase in the segment for radio. Don't let the segment settle into a Bella-as-feminist-awakening consensus; Daniel's provocation that she trades one servitude for another should stay uncomfortable. The Harmon manipulation question (c30:p22) is the most volatile cross-engagement point — save it for when energy needs a spike.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel's reading of c49:p74 (Wilfer blessing economic submission) directly contradicts Edmund's reading (Wilfer witnessing genuine moral conversion) — put these two in direct dialogue as early as the second question
Oliver's claim that the text 'knows' Harmon's deception is manipulative vs Daniel's claim that Dickens is unconsciously vindicating it — this is a genuine interpretive fork that can run hot

Edmund's resistance to any systemic reading of c18:p149 vs Daniel's insistence that it is the novel's truest anatomy of class — both are quoting the same passage to opposite ends, which makes for great radio

Oliver's 'mechanical men' thesis (Eugene's father, Boffin, Harmon all predetermined) is a bridge between Edmund's moral individualism and Daniel's structural critique — use Oliver to either reconcile or sharpen the conflict depending on the energy in the room

segment_name: The Comic Grotesque: Dickens's Laughter in the Dark

questions.question: Oliver, you've said we have to *hear* this stuff to get it — so let's start there. Can you actually read us that 'He do the Police in different voices' line and tell us why the grammar is doing something that a corrected version simply couldn't do?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform the passage (c16:p31) and establish the 'Dickens as performer' frame that will immediately create friction with Rosen's structural reading and Leigh's moral anatomy reading

questions.question: Daniel, you've described that same line as a 'double consciousness' — working-class speech performing institutional speech. But Oliver just gave us a reading about complicity and pleasure. Are those two things compatible, or is one of them letting Dickens off the hook?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Trevelyan's 'complicit pleasure' reading and Rosen's political reading of the same passage; draw out Rosen's strongest claim about laughter as ideological mechanism

questions.question: Edmund, I want to put you on the spot about the Deputy pocketing coins — you both want to quote that same moment from c41:p60, but you seem to want completely different things from it. Daniel sees systemic theft mirroring how property actually works; Oliver sees theatrical business about individual appetite. You say it's a surgical dissection of hypocrisy in the individual soul. Is there a version of this where you're all right, or does one reading actually cancel the others out?
questions.intent: Use the shared passage as a collision point for all three readings; force Leigh to defend the moral-individual reading against the structural and theatrical readings simultaneously; likely to produce the sharpest three-way disagreement

questions.question: Daniel, let's go to c40:p72 — Wegg's 'moral bondage and slavery.' You've said Wegg is articulating the logic of capital with terrifying clarity. But Edmund would say Wegg is just one man's theatrical hunger for dominion — he's not Capital, he's Wegg. Why does it matter which of you is right?
questions.intent: Draw out Rosen's most provocative claim about Wegg as structural rather than individual; invite Leigh to counter-punch; stakes the interpretive disagreement explicitly

questions.question: Oliver, you said the darkness in this comedy isn't nihilism — it's clarity. But Daniel's essentially arguing the laughter is the price we pay for seeing something true and terrible about the whole system. Are those the same thing described differently, or is one of you saying Dickens is more comfortable to read than he should be?
questions.intent: Close the segment by pushing on what 'dark' actually means across all three readings; force Trevelyan to either defend his 'genuine delight' position or concede ground to Rosen's more uncomfortable account; good closing tension

steering_notes: The real engine of this segment is the three-way split on what the laughter *does*: Trevelyan says it implicates and delights, Leigh says it dissects the individual moral will, Rosen says it exposes structural violence. All three keep coming back to the same two or three passages — that's the gift. Push them to fight over the same text rather than retreating to different examples. Watch for Leigh and Rosen to talk past each other (individual vs. systemic) — name that gap explicitly and make them address it directly. Trevelyan is the most likely to be a peacemaker; don't let him synthesise too early. The best radio moment will be when someone accuses another of making Dickens more comfortable than he is.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen and Leigh both want to quote 'I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow' (c41:p60) but for opposite reasons — Leigh sees individual hypocrisy, Rosen sees structural performance. Name this explicitly and make them both account for the same words.

Trevelyan's 'complicity and pleasure' thesis and Rosen's 'laughter as ideological mechanism' thesis are in genuine tension — one implies the reader is enriched by laughing, the other implies they may be implicated in what they're laughing at. This is the sharpest cross-engagement in the segment.

Leigh's insistence that Wegg is 'one man's moral imagination' directly contradicts Rosen's reading of the 'halves' scheme as mirroring how property and law actually function — this is a concrete, textual disagreement that can be resolved by looking at the passage together.

Trevelyan and Leigh both resist systemic readings but for different reasons: Trevelyan because he thinks individual appetite is the real story, Leigh because he thinks Dickens is a moralist not a propagandist. They may find themselves allied against Rosen but should be encouraged to acknowledge their own disagreement about what morality in fiction is actually for.

segment_name: Society's Mirrors: How Character Reveals Class

questions.question: Oliver, you've said we have to actually read Twemlow aloud to feel what Dickens is doing—so let's start there. Can you give us the dining-table line and tell us why you think it's comedy first, not critique?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the Twemlow passage (c2:p2) and land his central claim that the furniture metaphor is comedy *that is* the critique—sets up immediate friction with both Edmund and Daniel who read it as moral anatomy and structural indictment respectively

questions.question: Daniel, you've called Twemlow 'complicit'—which is a pretty aggressive word for a man the novel explicitly calls innocent. Oliver's just argued he's a comic figure, a tool. You're saying he's more like a collaborator. Make the case.
questions.intent: Force Daniel to defend the complicity reading against both Oliver's comic-tool framing and Edmund's moral-passivity reading—should produce triangular disagreement about where responsibility sits

questions.question: Edmund, you've said Bradley Headstone murders because he lacks self-mastery—that this is about individual moral failure, not the system. Daniel's going to tell you that's the sentimental reading Dickens is actively undercutting. Who's right about what Dickens is actually asking us to feel when we watch Bradley fall apart?
questions.intent: Direct confrontation between Edmund's moral-anatomy reading and Daniel's structural reading—draws out Edmund's strongest claim about the novel being about soul education not social diagnosis

questions.question: Oliver, you want to call Bradley a grotesque rather than a tragic figure—but Edmund just used the phrase 'moral imagination of the highest order' about that blood passage in c51. When Dickens writes 'the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven'—is that gothic entertainment, or has Dickens actually earned something tragic there?
questions.intent: Push Oliver on his pushback against the tragic register—forces him to either concede Dickens shifts gears in that passage or defend the grotesque-comic reading against Edmund's high moral tone, potentially opening space for Daniel to complicate both

questions.question: Let's end on Charley's line—'you are in all your passions so selfish and so concentrated upon yourself.' All three of you want to quote it, which means you're all reading it differently. Daniel, you've said the Charley scene is about what happens when intimacy inside the system is withdrawn. Edmund thinks it's a straightforward moral indictment. Oliver thinks it's a performance moment where an actor has to *feel* it land. Can those three readings coexist, or does one of them kill the others?
questions.intent: Use the shared passage (c57:p86) as a lightning rod to bring all three readings into direct comparison—ideal closing question because it either produces synthesis or a satisfying three-way disagreement about what the novel fundamentally is

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension that should be kept live rather than resolved: Oliver (performance/grotesque/comedy), Edmund (individual moral anatomy), Daniel (structural critique/complicity). Resist any drift toward consensus—if they start agreeing, push on Twemlow's innocence or Bradley's sympathy. The shared passages are a gift: all three experts want to quote the same lines for completely different reasons, so use that as a recurring device. Keep Oliver performing; keep Edmund precise and a little severe; let Daniel be the most politically charged voice in the room. Aim for the segment to end with the Charley line as an open question rather than a resolved argument.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's claim that Twemlow is a 'tool' vs Daniel's claim he is 'complicit'—these look similar but have opposite moral implications for Twemlow himself; push them to identify exactly where they diverge

Edmund's reading of Bradley's collapse as individual moral failure directly contradicts Daniel's structural reading—the blood passage (c51:p62) is the flashpoint, since both want to quote it and both claim it supports their opposing positions

Oliver's insistence on the grotesque-comic register for Bradley sits uneasily with Edmund's 'moral imagination of the highest order'—Oliver should be asked directly whether he thinks Edmund is over-reading

Daniel's complicity argument about Twemlow runs against the novel's own word 'innocent'—Edmund will likely defend that word on moral grounds, Oliver on comic-performance grounds; three-way split on a single authorial adjective is good radio

segment_name: Closing: Dust to Ashes, Self to Self

questions.question: Oliver, you said before we started that John Harmon 'doesn't know himself'—that after all those selves, the exile, the sailor, the secretary, the real John Harmon might simply not exist. So what do we make of the confession? Is that scene Dickens letting him off the hook, or is the whole point that even the confession is just another performance?
questions.intent: Draw out Oliver's strongest take—the radical idea that sincerity is itself a performance—and set up immediate tension with Edmund's reading of the confession as genuine moral reckoning

questions.question: Daniel, you quoted that line—'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses'—and I want to push on that. You're saying Harmon treats disguise as a gentleman's game. But doesn't Dickens at least make him pay for it, somewhere? Or does he genuinely get away clean?
questions.intent: Force Daniel to confront whether the novel has any critique of Harmon baked in, or whether the ending fully launders him—this should provoke Edmund to defend Harmon's conscience and Oliver to complicate both

questions.question: Edmund, all three of you want to quote the same line—Sloppy as 'a perfect Argus in the way of buttons, shining and winking and gleaming.' You say it's about the soul's inability to fit itself into the world. Daniel says it's about class being literally unwearable on the body. Who's right, or is that even the right question?
questions.intent: Force the central disagreement about the Sloppy passage into direct collision—Edmund's moral-universalist reading versus Daniel's structural reading—and give Oliver space to play referee with his 'comedy is the pathos' argument

questions.question: Here's something that's been nagging at me. You said Sloppy is 'the only honest character in the novel'—that he's permanently marked, that the kindness is the trap. But Oliver would say the comedy of that suit is the pathos, that Dickens is showing real kindness as visibly awkward. Aren't you two actually saying the same thing from opposite directions—and if so, does that mean the novel is more honest about its own limitations than you're giving it credit for?
questions.intent: Create a moment where Daniel and Oliver are forced to recognise their convergence—both see the suit as tragedy—but keep pressure on whether Dickens intended that or stumbled into it

questions.question: Edmund, last one, and I'll put it bluntly: Daniel says Harmon's confession costs him nothing—he's already rich, he confesses, and he ends up exactly where he started. You say it's a genuine portrait of conscience. Can you square that circle? Is there any reading of this ending where Dickens isn't letting the wealthy characters have it both ways?
questions.intent: End the segment on the sharpest possible version of the disagreement—Edmund is forced to either defend the novel's moral structure or concede Daniel's critique has real bite, while Oliver's 'authenticity as performance' thesis hangs over the whole exchange as a possible escape route

steering_notes: This segment should feel like it's building toward something that doesn't quite resolve—which is appropriate given the novel's own refusal to settle. Let the Sloppy passage anchor the first half and the Harmon confession anchor the second. The key tension is between Edmund's moral-universalist reading and Daniel's structural-political one, with Oliver as a genuinely useful third position that sometimes cuts across both. Don't let Edmund and Daniel talk past each other—push them to name the specific thing they disagree on. The best radio moment will come if Edmund is forced to say whether the ending is generous or evasive. End on ambiguity, not verdict.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver and Daniel converge on Sloppy as tragedy but from opposite directions—Oliver sees Dickens intending the pathos, Daniel sees Dickens unable to escape it. Push them to name the difference explicitly.

Edmund's 'soul unable to fit itself into the world' and Daniel's 'class being literally unwearable' use almost identical imagery for opposite ends—point this out and let them fight over whether it matters.
All three experts want to quote the Argus-buttons passage but read it completely differently—this is the single best cross-engagement moment in the segment, let it run.

Daniel's claim that confession 'costs Harmon nothing' directly contradicts Oliver's reading that the prose refuses to let Harmon justify himself—Oliver should be invited to respond to Daniel here specifically.
